title: 🌡️ Heat Transfer Lab
description: Welcome to the Heat Transfer Lab! You are a Grade 7 student who has been selected to join the school's Advanced Thermal Science Program. Over 14 weeks, you will explore conduction, convection, and radiation — the three ways heat moves through matter and space. From cooking experiments to building insulation models, you will discover how thermal energy shapes our everyday world. Can you master all three modes of heat transfer and earn the title of Thermal Scientist?
subject: physics
how_to_play: You are a Grade 7 student exploring heat transfer over a 14-week advanced science program.
Each week presents a thermal challenge with choices that affect your knowledge, safety, and experimental skills.
Watch your dashboard — your Lab Stations (Safety, Conduction Bench, Convection Chamber, Radiation Station, Analysis Lab) are interconnected.
NPCs like Dr. Kelvin (teacher), Thermo (lab assistant AI), Priya, and Arjun react to your decisions.
Random events like heatwave simulations and guest scientists will test your adaptability.
Keep your Safety Rating high — working with heat sources requires constant vigilance!
learning_objectives: Understand the three modes of heat transfer: conduction, convection, and radiation
Identify conductors and insulators and explain their thermal properties
Explain how thermal equilibrium is reached between objects at different temperatures
Design experiments to measure and compare heat transfer rates
Apply heat transfer concepts to real-world scenarios like cooking, clothing, and building design
Develop safe laboratory practices when working with heat sources
cultural_context: School science laboratory, hands-on thermal experiments, real-world applications of heat transfer

rounds.situation: Welcome to the Thermal Science Program! Dr. Kelvin greets the class: 'Heat is energy in transit — it always flows from hot objects to cold ones, never the other way around. Today we begin our journey to understand the three ways heat travels: conduction, convection, and radiation.' The lab is set up with Bunsen burners, metal rods, water baths, and infrared lamps. How do you want to start?
rounds.goal: Begin understanding heat energy and the three modes of heat transfer.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Building a strong foundation in thermal concepts now will make every future experiment more meaningful.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does heat always flow from hot to cold? Can you think of everyday examples?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 7 students entering a physics lab with Bunsen burners and thermometers on benches, teacher at whiteboard drawing heat transfer diagrams, warm welcoming light

choices.label: A. Heat is the transfer of thermal energy from a hotter object to a cooler object due to a temperature difference between them
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Heat is thermal energy in transit — it always flows from a hotter object to a cooler one. This happens because fast-moving particles in the hot object collide with slower particles in the cold object, transferring kinetic energy. Heat flow stops when both objects reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. Heat and temperature are the same thing — both measure how hot an object is
choices.feedback: 💡 Common misconception! Heat and temperature are NOT the same. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles in an object (how fast they vibrate). Heat is the transfer of thermal energy between objects at different temperatures. A swimming pool at 30°C has much more heat energy than a cup of tea at 70°C, even though the tea has a higher temperature.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. Heat can flow from a cold object to a hot object if the cold object is larger in size
choices.feedback: 💡 Not quite! Heat ALWAYS flows from hot to cold, regardless of the size of the objects. A large block of ice will never warm up a small cup of hot water — instead, the hot water loses heat to the ice. Size affects how MUCH heat transfers and how long it takes, but never the direction.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Heat is a type of substance that flows out of hot objects like invisible liquid
choices.feedback: 💡 This was actually believed for centuries! Scientists once thought heat was an invisible fluid called 'caloric' that flowed between objects. We now know heat is NOT a substance — it is the transfer of kinetic energy between particles. When you heat a metal rod, the particles vibrate faster and bump into their neighbours, passing energy along.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: This week focuses on conduction — heat transfer through direct contact between particles. Dr. Kelvin demonstrates by placing different metal rods (copper, iron, aluminum, steel) with wax drops at the far end into hot water. 'Watch which wax melts first — that tells you which metal conducts heat best!' Priya is fascinated, while Arjun already has his data table ready.
rounds.goal: Understand conduction and compare heat conductivity of different materials.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Predicting which material conducts best before testing helps you develop scientific intuition.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does a metal spoon feel colder than a wooden spoon at the same room temperature?
rounds.image_prompt: Close-up of metal rods in hot water with wax drops melting at different rates, student recording observations, colorful metals, steam rising

choices.label: A. Metals are good conductors because their particles are closely packed and they have free electrons that carry energy quickly
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Metals like copper and aluminum are excellent heat conductors for two reasons: (1) their atoms are tightly packed, so vibrations pass quickly from atom to atom, and (2) they have free electrons that can zoom through the metal carrying energy. This is why a metal spoon in hot soup gets hot fast but a wooden spoon stays cool!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. Wood conducts heat better than copper because wood is a natural material and natural materials transfer energy more efficiently
choices.feedback: 💡 Actually, the opposite is true! Copper is one of the BEST heat conductors, while wood is an insulator. Being 'natural' has nothing to do with conductivity. What matters is how particles are arranged: copper has free electrons and tightly packed atoms, while wood has loosely bonded molecules with trapped air pockets that resist heat flow.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Conduction works by hot air molecules rising upward and carrying heat energy to cooler regions
choices.feedback: 💡 You are describing convection, not conduction! In conduction, particles do NOT move from place to place — they vibrate in position and pass energy to their neighbours through direct contact, like a line of people passing a ball. Convection is when hot fluid (liquid or gas) physically moves, carrying heat with it.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. A metal spoon feels colder than a plastic spoon at room temperature because the metal is actually at a lower temperature
choices.feedback: 💡 Tricky misconception! Both spoons are at the SAME room temperature. The metal feels colder because it conducts heat AWAY from your warm hand much faster than plastic. Your skin senses the rate of heat loss, not the actual temperature. This is why metal park benches feel freezing in winter while wooden ones feel less cold.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: This week is all about convection — heat transfer through the movement of fluids (liquids and gases). Dr. Kelvin heats a beaker of water with a drop of food coloring at the bottom. 'Watch the color rise!' he says. 'Hot fluid rises, cool fluid sinks, creating a convection current — a circular flow that carries heat through the liquid.' The lab fills with the smell of warm water and excitement.
rounds.goal: Understand convection currents and how heat moves through liquids and gases.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Convection requires thinking in 3D — hot things rise, cool things sink. Switching from 1D conduction thinking to 3D convection thinking shows mental flexibility.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How do convection currents help distribute heat in your home? Think about radiators and air conditioning.
rounds.image_prompt: Beaker of water on a hot plate with food coloring showing circular convection current, arrows drawn on glass showing flow pattern, student observing closely

choices.label: A. In convection, hot fluid rises because heating makes it less dense than the cooler fluid around it
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When fluid (liquid or gas) is heated, its particles move faster and spread apart, making the fluid less dense. This less dense hot fluid rises while cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place, creating a convection current. This is how radiators heat a room and why hot air balloons float!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Convection can happen in solids, liquids, and gases because all materials have particles that can move freely
choices.feedback: 💡 Convection does NOT happen in solids! For convection to occur, particles must be free to move from one place to another, which only happens in fluids (liquids and gases). In solids, particles are locked in fixed positions and can only vibrate — that is conduction, not convection.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Sea breezes blow from the land to the sea during the daytime because land heats up slower than water
choices.feedback: 💡 This is reversed! During the day, land heats up FASTER than water (land has lower specific heat capacity). Hot air over the land rises, and cooler air from the sea rushes in to replace it — creating a sea breeze that blows FROM the sea TO the land. At night, the pattern reverses because land cools faster.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Hot water sinks to the bottom of a pot because heat energy makes water heavier and denser
choices.feedback: 💡 The opposite is true! Heating makes water LESS dense because the particles spread apart. Hot water rises to the top, not sinks. That is why the top of bath water can feel warm while the bottom is still cool. The only exception is water below 4°C, which behaves unusually — ice floats because frozen water is less dense than liquid water!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.round_title: Week 4: Radiation — Heat Through Empty Space
rounds.situation: The third and final mode! Dr. Kelvin turns off the lights and turns on an infrared heat lamp. 'Feel the warmth on your face — but there is no air blowing and nothing touching you. The heat is traveling as invisible electromagnetic waves through empty space. This is radiation!' He explains that this is how the Sun heats Earth across 150 million kilometers of vacuum.
rounds.goal: Understand thermal radiation and how heat can travel without any medium.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Radiation from the Sun sustains all life on Earth. Understanding energy transfer connects science to environmental responsibility.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How is the Sun's heat different from the heat you feel when touching a hot cup? What makes radiation special?
rounds.image_prompt: Student feeling warmth from an infrared heat lamp in a darkened lab, red glow visible, thermal imaging camera showing heat patterns on the wall

choices.label: A. Radiation is the only mode of heat transfer that does not need a medium — it can travel through the vacuum of space
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Unlike conduction and convection, which need particles to transfer energy, radiation travels as electromagnetic waves (infrared radiation). These waves can travel through empty space at the speed of light. This is how the Sun's heat reaches Earth across 150 million km of vacuum — neither conduction nor convection could do this!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Dark-coloured surfaces reflect more thermal radiation than light-coloured surfaces, which is why we wear dark clothes in summer
choices.feedback: 💡 This is backwards! Dark surfaces ABSORB more radiation and reflect less, while light surfaces REFLECT more and absorb less. That is why wearing white or light-coloured clothes in summer keeps you cooler — they reflect the Sun's radiation. Dark clothes absorb it and make you hotter.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Radiation only travels from very hot objects like the Sun or fire — everyday warm objects do not emit radiation
choices.feedback: 💡 Every object with a temperature above absolute zero (−273°C) emits thermal radiation! Your body, a warm cup of tea, even an ice cube emits infrared radiation. Hotter objects emit more radiation, but ALL objects emit some. Thermal imaging cameras can detect the radiation from your body, walls, and electronics — everything is glowing in infrared!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Shiny aluminium foil is used as insulation because it absorbs all the radiation and traps it inside
choices.feedback: 💡 Almost right reasoning, but wrong mechanism! Shiny aluminium foil works as insulation because it REFLECTS radiation, not absorbs it. Its shiny surface bounces thermal radiation back instead of letting it pass through. That is why emergency blankets are shiny — they reflect your body's heat radiation back to you.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Dr. Kelvin holds up a thermos flask: 'This is one of the greatest inventions in heat transfer engineering. It uses a vacuum to prevent conduction and convection, a shiny surface to reduce radiation, and an insulated cap to minimize all three modes.' This week you explore what makes materials good conductors or insulators and design your own insulation solutions.
rounds.goal: Understand thermal conductors and insulators and apply knowledge to insulation design.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Insulators do not stop heat — they slow it down. Understanding the difference between blocking and delaying is a key thinking skill.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do we wrap ice cream in newspaper to keep it frozen? How does an insulator work at the particle level?
rounds.image_prompt: Cross-section of a thermos flask showing vacuum layer and reflective coating, student examining various insulation materials, wool, styrofoam, bubble wrap on table

choices.label: A. Wool and foam are good insulators because they trap tiny pockets of air, and air is a very poor conductor of heat
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The secret of most insulators is trapped air. Air molecules are far apart and cannot easily pass vibrations, making air a terrible conductor. Materials like wool, foam, feathers, and bubble wrap work by trapping millions of tiny air pockets. This is also why double-glazed windows have an air gap between the glass panes!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: B. A thermos flask keeps drinks hot by using thick glass walls that block all three types of heat transfer equally
choices.feedback: 💡 A thermos is more clever than thick glass! It uses THREE different strategies: (1) a vacuum between the walls eliminates conduction and convection (no particles), (2) shiny silver coating reflects radiation back, and (3) an insulated stopper reduces heat escape from the top. Each part targets a different mode of heat transfer!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. Metals are good insulators of heat, which is why cooking pots are made of metal — to keep heat inside the pot
choices.feedback: 💡 Metals are CONDUCTORS, not insulators! Cooking pots are made of metal precisely because metal conducts heat efficiently from the stove into the food. If pots were made of an insulator like wood, the heat would never reach the food. Notice that pot HANDLES are made of plastic or wood (insulators) so you can hold them without burning your hands!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. Insulators completely stop all heat transfer, which is why insulated objects never cool down
choices.feedback: 💡 Insulators SLOW DOWN heat transfer but never stop it completely. Even the best thermos flask eventually lets your tea go cold — it just takes much longer. No material is a perfect insulator. Given enough time, all objects will reach thermal equilibrium with their surroundings. Insulators simply buy you more time.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: Dr. Kelvin places a hot metal block into a cup of cold water. 'Watch the temperatures — the metal cools down and the water warms up. Eventually they reach the same temperature. We call this thermal equilibrium.' He challenges the class to predict the final temperature and understand energy conservation in heat transfer.
rounds.goal: Understand thermal equilibrium and energy conservation during heat transfer.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Equilibrium is about balance. In life, as in physics, systems naturally move toward balance — understanding this helps you predict outcomes.
rounds.reflection_prompt: If you mix hot and cold water, will the final temperature be exactly in the middle? Why or why not?
rounds.image_prompt: Metal block being placed into water with two thermometers showing converging temperatures, graph on paper showing temperature curves meeting, student recording data

choices.label: A. When a hot metal block is placed in cold water, both reach the same final temperature because energy lost by the metal equals energy gained by the water
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ This is the principle of conservation of energy in heat transfer. The hot metal loses exactly as much thermal energy as the cold water gains. Heat flows from the metal to the water until both reach the same temperature — this final state is called thermal equilibrium. The total energy in the system stays constant!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. If you mix 1 litre of water at 20°C with 1 litre of water at 80°C, the final temperature will always be exactly 50°C regardless of the container
choices.feedback: 💡 In a perfect, insulated world, yes — equal volumes at 20°C and 80°C would give 50°C. But in reality, some heat escapes to the container and the air (surroundings). The actual final temperature would be slightly below 50°C. Real experiments always lose some heat to the environment, which is why insulation matters!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. Two objects reach thermal equilibrium when they have the same amount of heat energy, even if their temperatures are different
choices.feedback: 💡 Thermal equilibrium means the objects are at the SAME TEMPERATURE, not the same amount of heat energy. A large ocean and a small cup can be at the same temperature (equilibrium) but the ocean has vastly more heat energy. Temperature equality is what stops heat flowing between them, not equal energy amounts.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. When hot and cold objects touch, the cold object gives its coldness to the hot object, making it cooler
choices.feedback: 💡 There is no such thing as 'coldness' being transferred! Only heat (thermal energy) moves, and it always flows from hot to cold. When you hold an ice cube, your hand feels cold because heat is flowing OUT of your hand INTO the ice — not because cold is flowing in.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: EMERGENCY! During today's experiment, a student accidentally touches a hot beaker straight from the Bunsen burner and gets a minor burn. The student is crying, others are panicking, and Dr. Kelvin rushes to help. 'First aid first, questions later,' he says firmly. After treating the burn under cold running water, he addresses the class: 'This is exactly why thermal safety is non-negotiable. Now — how do we make sure this never happens again?'
rounds.goal: Handle a thermal burn emergency and improve safety procedures.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Accidents test your character. Staying calm, knowing first aid, and learning from mistakes separates responsible scientists from careless ones.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What should you always do FIRST if someone gets burned? Why is cold running water the best immediate treatment?
rounds.image_prompt: School science lab with first aid being administered, student holding hand under cold running water, concerned teacher and classmates, safety poster visible on wall

choices.label: A. Running cold water over a burn for at least 10 minutes is the correct first aid because it removes heat energy from the skin and reduces tissue damage
choices.learning_concept: Burns and Heat Transfer First Aid
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Cold running water works by conducting heat away from the burned skin rapidly. The water absorbs thermal energy from the burn site, lowering the temperature and preventing deeper tissue damage. It must be cool (not ice-cold) water for at least 10 minutes. Never apply ice, butter, or toothpaste — these can make burns worse!

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Standing by your values even under pressure builds integrity.

choices.label: B. Applying ice directly to a burn is the best treatment because ice is the coldest thing available and will cool the burn fastest
choices.feedback: 💡 Dangerous misconception! Ice can actually cause ADDITIONAL damage to burned skin. Ice is so cold (0°C or below) that it can cause frostbite on already damaged tissue. The extreme temperature difference can also restrict blood flow. Cool running water (around 15°C) is much safer.

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Thinking about what's fair for everyone involved shows ethical awareness.

choices.label: C. Glass beakers can never cause burns because glass is an insulator and does not conduct heat
choices.feedback: 💡 Glass is a poor conductor compared to metals, but it still conducts enough heat to cause serious burns! A glass beaker heated on a Bunsen burner can be well above 100°C. Always use tongs and check if glassware has been heated before touching it.

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Choosing what's right over what's easy shows moral courage.

choices.label: D. You can tell if a lab object is hot by how it looks — hot objects always glow red or give off visible steam
choices.feedback: 💡 Very dangerous assumption! Objects can be dangerously hot (200-300°C) without glowing or producing visible steam. In the lab, ALWAYS assume an object near a heat source might be hot. Use the back of your hand near (not touching) the object to feel for radiated heat.

skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Considering fairness in your decision demonstrates ethical thinking.

rounds.situation: Dr. Kelvin brings a surprise to the lab — a portable kitchen setup! 'Cooking is the world's most popular heat transfer experiment,' he announces with a grin. 'Today we analyze cooking methods through the lens of physics. Boiling uses convection, frying uses conduction, and grilling uses radiation. Let us investigate how heat transforms food!'
rounds.goal: Apply heat transfer knowledge to analyze and compare cooking methods.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Seeing familiar things (cooking) through a scientific lens is a superpower. The best scientists find physics in everyday life.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does food cook faster in a pressure cooker? How does changing pressure affect boiling point and heat transfer?
rounds.image_prompt: Lab setup with cooking experiments, pot of boiling water with thermometer, frying pan with oil, and a small grill, students recording temperatures and observations

choices.label: A. Boiling water stays at exactly 100°C no matter how high you turn the flame, because the extra energy goes into changing water from liquid to gas (steam)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Once water reaches 100°C, additional heat energy does NOT raise the temperature further. Instead, the energy breaks the bonds holding water molecules together, turning liquid into gas (steam). This energy is called 'latent heat of vaporisation'. A higher flame just makes water boil faster (more steam), not hotter!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. A pressure cooker cooks food faster because the increased pressure makes the flame hotter inside the cooker
choices.feedback: 💡 The flame stays the same! A pressure cooker works because increased pressure raises the boiling point of water above 100°C (to about 120°C). Since the water can now get hotter before boiling, food cooks faster. This is why food at high altitudes (low pressure) takes longer to cook!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Frying food in oil works because oil is a better insulator than water and traps more heat inside the food
choices.feedback: 💡 Frying works because of conduction, not insulation! Oil can reach much higher temperatures than water (oil: 180-200°C vs water: max 100°C) without boiling. The hot oil conducts heat energy directly into the food's surface at these higher temperatures, which is why frying creates a crispy brown crust that boiling cannot achieve.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Grilling food uses convection as the main method of heat transfer because hot air from the grill rises into the food
choices.feedback: 💡 While some convection occurs, grilling mainly uses RADIATION. The hot coals or heating element emit infrared radiation that travels directly to the food's surface without needing air as a medium. Boiling uses convection, frying uses conduction, and grilling uses radiation.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: Dr. Kelvin lights a candle on a lab bench and asks: 'How many modes of heat transfer can you identify right now?' The answer is ALL THREE — the wax melts by conduction, hot air rises by convection, and you feel warmth on your face from radiation. This week's challenge: analyze real-world systems where all three modes work together simultaneously.
rounds.goal: Analyze systems where conduction, convection, and radiation all operate together.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Real problems involve multiple principles working simultaneously. Breaking complex situations into components is the key to understanding.
rounds.reflection_prompt: In a bonfire, where does each type of heat transfer occur? Can you identify all three?
rounds.image_prompt: Candle flame on a lab bench with arrows showing three modes — conduction through wax, convection of hot air rising, radiation warming nearby surfaces, student diagramming

choices.label: A. A burning candle demonstrates all three modes: conduction melts the wax, convection carries hot air upward, and radiation warms your face from a distance
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A candle is a perfect example of all three modes working together. Conduction: heat travels down the wick and melts nearby wax. Convection: hot gases rise above the flame (that is why a candle flame points up). Radiation: you feel warmth on your face even from a distance. Most real-world situations involve all three modes!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. In a room with a radiator, heat only reaches you through radiation since the device is called a 'radiator'
choices.feedback: 💡 Despite the name, home radiators mainly heat a room through CONVECTION! The radiator heats the air touching it (conduction), then warm air rises and circulates around the room (convection). Some radiation occurs too, but convection is the dominant mode. The name 'radiator' is actually misleading!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Heat can only travel by one mode at a time — when conduction is happening, convection and radiation must stop
choices.feedback: 💡 All three modes can happen simultaneously! When you hold a hot cup of tea: conduction heats your hands through the cup, convection carries hot steam upward, and radiation lets you feel warmth near the cup without touching it. In most real situations, all three modes operate at once.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. The human body only loses heat through conduction when touching cold objects — we do not lose heat through convection or radiation
choices.feedback: 💡 Your body loses heat through ALL three modes plus evaporation! Conduction: sitting on a cold chair. Convection: wind chill removes warm air from your skin. Radiation: your body constantly radiates infrared heat. Evaporation: sweating cools you as water absorbs energy to become gas.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

rounds.situation: Dr. Kelvin pours equal amounts of water and cooking oil into identical beakers and heats them together. 'Watch the thermometers,' he says. The oil temperature shoots up twice as fast as the water! 'Different substances need different amounts of heat to warm up. We call this specific heat capacity.' He writes the formula on the board: Q = m × c × ΔT.
rounds.goal: Understand specific heat capacity and its role in heat transfer calculations.
rounds.coaching_moment: Ethical reasoning: Water's high specific heat capacity is why oceans regulate Earth's climate. Understanding this connects physics to environmental science.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why does sand at the beach get burning hot while the ocean stays cool? What does this tell you about specific heat capacity?
rounds.image_prompt: Two beakers on hot plates — one with water, one with oil — showing different thermometer readings, student plotting temperature vs time graph, formula Q=mcΔT on whiteboard

choices.label: A. Water has a very high specific heat capacity, which means it needs a lot of energy to warm up and releases a lot of energy when cooling down
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Water's specific heat capacity is 4,200 J/kg°C — one of the highest of any common substance. This means 1 kg of water needs 4,200 joules of energy to warm by just 1°C. This is why oceans keep coastal cities at moderate temperatures, why car engines use water as coolant, and why a hot water bottle stays warm for hours!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: B. Sand at the beach gets hotter than seawater in the sun because sand absorbs more sunlight than water does
choices.feedback: 💡 Both sand and water absorb similar amounts of sunlight, but sand heats up MUCH faster because it has a LOWER specific heat capacity (about 830 J/kg°C vs water's 4,200 J/kg°C). The same solar energy raises sand's temperature about 5 times more than water's.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. If you heat 1 kg of water and 1 kg of oil with the same energy, the water will get hotter because water absorbs heat better
choices.feedback: 💡 It is the opposite! Oil has a LOWER specific heat capacity than water, so the oil will get hotter. Water's HIGH specific heat means it 'resists' temperature change. When you give the same energy to both, the substance with lower specific heat (oil) shows a bigger temperature rise.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Specific heat capacity depends only on the temperature of the substance, not on what the substance is made of
choices.feedback: 💡 Specific heat capacity is a property of the MATERIAL itself, not its temperature. Water always has about 4,200 J/kg°C whether at 10°C or 90°C. Iron has about 450 J/kg°C. Each substance has its own unique value determined by its molecular structure.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Dr. Kelvin announces a team competition: 'Each team will design, build, and present a thermal device that solves a real problem using heat transfer principles. Your device must demonstrate at least two modes of heat transfer. The best project earns the Thermal Engineer trophy!' Priya and Arjun are fired up. This is your chance to combine everything!
rounds.goal: Collaborate to design and build a practical thermal device.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: Great teams leverage everyone's strengths. The best projects come from teams where every voice is heard and valued.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What role did you play in your team, and how did understanding heat transfer help your design?
rounds.image_prompt: Team of Grade 7 students collaborating on a thermal device project, one sketching diagrams, one assembling materials, one testing with thermometer, energetic teamwork

choices.label: A. A solar water heater works by using a black surface to absorb radiation, then heating water by conduction, with insulation to prevent heat loss
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ A solar water heater combines multiple heat transfer principles: (1) a dark/black collector plate absorbs maximum solar radiation, (2) the absorbed heat transfers to water by conduction, (3) hot water rises and cold water sinks creating natural convection circulation, and (4) insulation reduces heat loss. This is smart engineering!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.creativity: Exploring an unconventional approach shows creative thinking.

choices.label: B. Double-glazed windows reduce heat loss mainly by having thicker glass that blocks conduction better than single glass
choices.feedback: 💡 The thickness of the glass is not the key feature! Double glazing works because of the AIR GAP trapped between the two panes. This air gap is a poor conductor. It also prevents convection currents from carrying heat across the gap. It is the trapped air that does the insulating work!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. An energy-efficient house should have small windows because all heat escapes through windows by convection only
choices.feedback: 💡 Heat escapes through windows by ALL THREE modes! Conduction: through the glass. Convection: draughts around frames. Radiation: infrared passes through glass. Modern windows use double/triple glazing (conduction), sealed frames (convection), and low-emissivity coatings (radiation).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. Painting a house white in a hot climate makes no difference to indoor temperature because paint cannot block heat
choices.feedback: 💡 Surface colour makes a significant difference! White paint reflects up to 80% of solar radiation, while dark paint absorbs most of it. White-roofed buildings can be 10-15°C cooler inside. This is why traditional houses in hot regions (Greece, Rajasthan) are painted white — radiation reflection is ancient building science!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

rounds.situation: CRISIS! When you arrive at the lab, you discover that the hot plates are not working, half the thermometers are giving wrong readings, and the supply cabinet is nearly empty. Budget cuts mean no replacements until next month. Dr. Kelvin looks worried: 'The Science Exhibition is two weeks away and we have barely any working equipment. How do we keep going?'
rounds.goal: Continue learning and project development despite severe equipment limitations.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: The greatest innovations often come from constraints. When resources are limited, creativity and teamwork become your most powerful tools.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Can limitations actually make you MORE creative? Think of a time when having less forced you to think differently.
rounds.image_prompt: Science lab with OUT OF ORDER signs on hot plates, nearly empty supply cabinet, students brainstorming solutions on whiteboard, determined expressions

choices.label: A. You can calibrate a thermometer using two fixed points: ice-water mixture at 0°C and boiling water at 100°C (at sea level)
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ These two temperatures are called 'fixed points' because they are reproducible and reliable. At standard atmospheric pressure, pure ice melts at exactly 0°C and pure water boils at exactly 100°C. By marking these two points and dividing the gap into 100 equal parts, you get the Celsius scale!

skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.
skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: B. The Kelvin temperature scale starts at 0 K, which is the temperature of ice, making it equivalent to 0°C
choices.feedback: 💡 0 Kelvin is NOT the same as 0°C! 0 K is absolute zero (−273°C), the coldest possible temperature where all particle motion theoretically stops. Ice melts at 273 K (= 0°C). To convert: K = °C + 273. The Kelvin scale is used in science because it starts at the true zero point of temperature.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: C. Mercury thermometers work because mercury changes colour when heated, turning from silver to red at high temperatures
choices.feedback: 💡 Mercury does not change colour! Thermometers work because liquids EXPAND when heated. As temperature rises, mercury expands and moves up the narrow tube. The red liquid in some thermometers is actually alcohol with red dye, not mercury. Both work on thermal expansion of liquids.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Water at 100°C on top of a mountain boils at the same rate as water at 100°C at sea level because the temperature is the same
choices.feedback: 💡 Here is the catch: water does not reach 100°C on a mountain top! At high altitudes, lower air pressure means water boils at a LOWER temperature (about 70°C on Mount Everest). This is why cooking takes much longer at high altitudes. Boiling point depends on pressure, not just the substance.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: One week before the Science Exhibition! Dr. Kelvin gives full creative freedom: 'Use everything you have learned about conduction, convection, and radiation to design the most innovative thermal application you can imagine. Think beyond the textbook — what real problem can heat transfer science solve?' The lab buzzes with final preparations and wild ideas.
rounds.goal: Push creativity and knowledge to design an original thermal innovation.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Innovation happens when you combine what you know in new ways. Every great invention started with a 'What if...?' question.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What is the most surprising thing you learned about heat transfer this semester? How could you use it to help someone?
rounds.image_prompt: Student sketching innovative thermal design in notebook, surrounded by insulation materials and prototypes, lightbulb moment, creative energy in the lab

choices.label: A. The greenhouse effect works because glass lets sunlight (short-wave radiation) in but traps infrared radiation (long-wave) emitted by warm objects inside
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Glass is transparent to visible light but blocks infrared radiation. Sunlight passes through, heats objects inside, and these warm objects emit infrared that cannot escape. Earth's atmosphere works similarly — CO2 and methane trap heat. This is why increasing greenhouse gases causes global warming!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.ethical_reasoning: Weighing the ethical implications shows principled reasoning.

choices.label: B. A solar cooker works by using a magnifying glass that creates fire from sunlight through the process of radiation conduction
choices.feedback: 💡 Solar cookers do not use magnifying glasses or create fire! They use curved reflective surfaces (mirrors) to concentrate sunlight onto a small cooking area. A black pot absorbs maximum radiation, and insulation prevents heat loss. 'Radiation conduction' is not a real term — radiation and conduction are separate modes.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Evaporation cools you down because the water on your skin absorbs cold from the surrounding air
choices.feedback: 💡 'Cold' cannot be absorbed — only heat can transfer! Evaporation cools you because liquid water needs energy to become vapour (latent heat). This energy comes from your SKIN, which loses thermal energy and feels cooler. Each gram of sweat that evaporates takes about 2,260 joules of heat from your body.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Energy-efficient buildings only need thick walls to prevent heat transfer — roof and floor insulation is unnecessary
choices.feedback: 💡 Heat escapes from ALL surfaces! Up to 25% of heat loss occurs through the ROOF (hot air rises by convection, escapes by conduction). About 10% through the floor. A truly efficient building insulates walls, roof, floor, windows, and seals gaps. Every surface matters!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: The Science Exhibition is here! The school hall is transformed with display boards, working models, and excited visitors — parents, other teachers, younger students, and even a judge from the district science board. Your thermal project is set up and ready. Dr. Kelvin says: 'This is your moment. Show the world what heat transfer can do.' How will you present your work?
rounds.goal: Present your thermal project at the Science Exhibition and showcase your journey.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Presenting your work to strangers takes courage. Whether you win or not, sharing knowledge with confidence is its own achievement.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Looking back at Week 1, how has your understanding of heat transfer changed? What would you tell your past self?
rounds.image_prompt: School Science Exhibition in a hall, students presenting thermal projects on display boards, parents and judges visiting, trophy on display, colorful decorations

choices.label: A. When solids are heated, they expand because their particles vibrate more and push further apart, which is why bridges have expansion gaps
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When heated, particles gain kinetic energy and vibrate more vigorously, pushing each other further apart. Bridges have expansion joints so metal can expand in summer without buckling. Railway tracks, power lines, and even the Eiffel Tower (which grows 15 cm taller in summer!) all account for thermal expansion.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Liquids expand more than solids when heated because liquid particles are heavier and gain more energy from heat
choices.feedback: 💡 Liquids DO expand more than solids, but not because their particles are heavier! Liquid particles are already more loosely bonded, so they have more freedom to move apart when heated. Gases expand even more. The order is: gases > liquids > solids. This has nothing to do with particle weight.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Water behaves like all other substances — it continuously contracts as it cools and is densest when frozen at 0°C
choices.feedback: 💡 Water is special! Unlike most substances, water is densest at 4°C, not 0°C. Below 4°C, water actually EXPANDS as it cools further, and ice is LESS dense than liquid water. This anomalous expansion is why ice floats and why ponds freeze from the top down, allowing fish to survive underneath!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Thermal expansion only matters in science laboratories — it has no practical importance in everyday engineering or construction
choices.feedback: 💡 Thermal expansion is critically important in engineering! Without expansion joints, bridges would buckle in summer. Railway tracks can bend dangerously. Power lines sag in heat. Even dental fillings must match the expansion rate of your teeth! Ignoring thermal expansion has caused real engineering disasters.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

glossary_terms.definition: The movement of thermal energy from a hotter object to a cooler object. Heat always flows from high temperature to low temperature until equilibrium is reached.
Heat transfer through direct contact between particles. Vibrating particles pass energy to neighboring particles. Works best in solids, especially metals.
Heat transfer through the movement of fluids (liquids or gases). Hot fluid rises and cool fluid sinks, creating circular convection currents that distribute heat.
Heat transfer through electromagnetic waves that can travel through empty space. No medium needed — this is how the Sun's heat reaches Earth across 150 million km.
The state reached when two objects in contact reach the same temperature and heat stops flowing between them. Energy is conserved throughout the process.
A material that allows heat to pass through it easily, like metals (copper, aluminum, iron). Metals conduct well because they have free electrons that carry energy quickly.
A material that resists heat flow, like wood, plastic, wool, and air. Insulators have tightly bound particles that do not pass energy easily.
The amount of heat energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1°C. Water has a very high specific heat capacity (4,200 J/kg°C).
A circular flow pattern in a fluid caused by heating. Hot fluid rises (less dense), cool fluid sinks (more dense), creating a continuous loop of moving fluid.
A measure of how well a material conducts heat. Copper has high thermal conductivity (385 W/m·K) while air has very low thermal conductivity (0.024 W/m·K).
A type of electromagnetic wave that carries thermal energy. All warm objects emit infrared radiation. Thermal imaging cameras detect this radiation to create heat maps.
The rate of heat loss of an object is proportional to the temperature difference between the object and its surroundings. Objects cool faster when the difference is large.

endings.title: Thermal Scientist
endings.message: You have achieved mastery in the Heat Transfer Lab! Your understanding of conduction, convection, and radiation is exceptional, your safety record is flawless, and your innovative thermal designs have amazed the school. Dr. Kelvin nominates you for the District Science Olympiad, and your solar cooker project is featured in the local newspaper. You have proven that understanding heat can change the world!

endings.title: Skilled Thermal Experimenter
endings.message: You have become a skilled thermal scientist with solid knowledge and good lab practices! Your Science Exhibition project demonstrates real competence in understanding and applying heat transfer. Dr. Kelvin is proud and says you are ready for the advanced physics program next year. Your future in science is bright and warm!

endings.title: Steady Learner
endings.message: You completed the Heat Transfer Program with mixed results. Some weeks were excellent and others were challenging, but you persisted and learned the fundamentals of how heat moves. Dr. Kelvin says there is always next semester to deepen your understanding, and the foundation you built will serve you well. Keep experimenting!

endings.title: Struggling Student
endings.message: The Heat Transfer Lab was a tough journey for you. Many concepts felt abstract, and the experiments did not always go as planned. But you did not give up. Dr. Kelvin arranges extra sessions and says: 'Students who struggle often develop the deepest understanding, because they have to fight for every insight.' Your thermal story is just beginning!

endings.title: Lab Safety Concern
endings.message: Due to repeated thermal safety violations, Dr. Kelvin has restricted your access to heat sources until you complete the Thermal Safety Certification. Burns are serious injuries that can scar for life. Thermo has prepared a personalized safety course for you. Master the safety protocols and come back stronger!

questions.question: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.explanation: Force is measured in Newtons (N), named after Sir Isaac Newton.

questions.question: What happens when balanced forces act on a stationary object?
questions.explanation: Balanced forces cancel out, so the object remains stationary.

questions.question: Friction always acts in which direction?
questions.explanation: Friction opposes the direction of motion or attempted motion.

questions.question: Friction always acts in which direction?

questions.question: Which of Newton's laws says 'every action has an equal and opposite reaction'?
questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
